title: Abilify and Alcohol: Risks, Timing, and What Your Label Says
excerpt: Can you drink on Abilify? How aripiprazole and alcohol interact, why timing your dose doesn't help, the risks for mood and judgment, and the warning signs that need care.
metaDescription: Can you drink on Abilify? How aripiprazole and alcohol interact, why dose timing doesn't help, side effects to watch for, and when to get help.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** the official advice is to avoid alcohol while you take Abilify (aripiprazole). The patient Medication Guide says so directly. That's not because one drink is known to be poisonous with it. It's because both Abilify and alcohol act on the brain, and together they can make you drowsier, dizzier, and less steady than either one alone, while alcohol can also undo some of the work Abilify is doing for your mood or thinking. The biggest practical risks are falls, driving while impaired, decisions you wouldn't normally make, and a rougher course for the condition you're treating.

**The quick rules:** Don't drink until you know how Abilify affects you, which usually means waiting until you've been on a steady dose for a few weeks. Never skip or stop a dose so you can drink; it doesn't clear your system quickly and stopping can bring symptoms back. If you and your prescriber decide an occasional drink is acceptable, keep it to one, have it with food, stay seated and hydrated, and never drive afterward. If drinking is something you do most weeks, tell your prescriber honestly. They can't adjust your treatment for something they don't know about.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research and label guidance. It is not a substitute for the doctor or pharmacist who knows your diagnosis, dose, and other medicines. **Talk to your prescriber before drinking on Abilify,** especially if you take it for bipolar disorder, take other sedating medicines, are over 65, or have a history of seizures, fainting, or heavy drinking. **Call 911 or go to the emergency room if** someone on Abilify who has been drinking can't be woken up, is breathing slowly or irregularly, faints, has a seizure, vomits while barely conscious, or develops a high fever with stiff muscles and confusion. If someone talks about harming themselves, call or text **988** (US Suicide and Crisis Lifeline) or 911.

## What Abilify Is and Why People Take It

Abilify is the brand name for **aripiprazole**, a prescription medicine in the group called atypical (or second-generation) antipsychotics. The name puts some people off, because "antipsychotic" sounds like it's only for psychosis. In practice aripiprazole is prescribed for a wider range of conditions. In the US it's approved for:

- **Schizophrenia**
- **Bipolar I disorder**, both to treat manic or mixed episodes and to help prevent new ones
- **Major depression**, as an add-on to an antidepressant when the antidepressant alone hasn't done enough
- **Irritability linked to autism** in children and teens
- **Tourette's disorder**

It also comes as long-acting injections given every month or two (sold as Abilify Maintena, Abilify Asimtufii, and Aristada, which is a related form called aripiprazole lauroxil). The interaction with alcohol is the same idea whether you take a daily tablet or get an injection.

### How it works, briefly

Most older antipsychotics simply block dopamine receptors. Aripiprazole is different. It's a **partial agonist** at dopamine D2 receptors, which means it partly switches the receptor on rather than fully blocking it. When dopamine signalling is too high, it turns it down; when it's too low, it nudges it up. That's why you'll sometimes hear it called a "dopamine stabilizer." It also acts on serotonin receptors (5-HT1A and 5-HT2A), which is part of why it helps with depression and mood.

That profile makes Abilify **less sedating than many drugs in its class**, such as quetiapine (Seroquel) or olanzapine. Plenty of people find it more activating than sleepy. But "less sedating" doesn't mean "not sedating." Sleepiness, dizziness, and restlessness are all common side effects on the label, and alcohol amplifies exactly those.

## How Abilify and Alcohol Interact: The Mechanism in Plain Words

There's no dramatic chemical reaction between aripiprazole and alcohol in the bloodstream. Alcohol doesn't meaningfully change how your liver breaks down aripiprazole, which is handled mainly by two liver enzymes called CYP2D6 and CYP3A4. The problem is what pharmacists call a **pharmacodynamic** interaction: the two substances act on the same systems in your brain and body, and their effects add up.

### 1. Stacked drowsiness and slowed reactions

Alcohol is a central nervous system depressant. It slows reaction time, coordination, and judgment. Abilify can cause sleepiness (the label calls it somnolence) and can affect thinking and motor skills, which is why the Medication Guide tells people not to drive or operate machinery until they know how it affects them. Put the two together and the impairment can be greater than you'd predict from the number of drinks. People often describe feeling "two drinks drunk after one."

### 2. Dizziness and fainting when you stand up

Abilify can lower blood pressure when you go from lying or sitting to standing (orthostatic hypotension), especially early in treatment or after a dose increase. Alcohol widens blood vessels and dehydrates you, which pushes blood pressure the same way. The result can be light-headedness, blurred vision, or fainting when you get up from the couch or out of bed at night. The aripiprazole label specifically lists **falls** as a risk, and alcohol makes falls more likely on its own.

### 3. Judgment, impulses, and compulsive urges

In 2016 the FDA added a warning to aripiprazole's label about **compulsive or uncontrollable urges**: gambling, binge eating, shopping, and sexual urges. These are uncommon, but they were serious enough to get a specific safety communication. Alcohol lowers inhibitions. If you've noticed any of these urges since starting Abilify, drinking is likely to make them harder to resist. Tell your prescriber about them either way, because they usually ease when the dose is lowered or the medicine is changed.

### 4. Restlessness (akathisia) and sleep

One of Abilify's most common side effects is **akathisia**, an inner restlessness that makes it hard to sit still. It's especially common when aripiprazole is added for depression. Some people find that a drink seems to take the edge off that restlessness in the evening. That's worth mentioning to your prescriber rather than managing on your own, because alcohol fragments sleep in the second half of the night and tends to leave you more on edge the next day. If restlessness is the reason you're reaching for a drink, there are medical fixes for akathisia.

### 5. Body temperature and dehydration

The label warns that antipsychotics, including aripiprazole, can interfere with the body's ability to cool itself, and advises avoiding overheating and dehydration. Drinking makes you lose fluid and can dull your sense of being too hot. A long day drinking outdoors in summer, or dancing in a hot club, is a situation where this matters.

## What the Label and Official Guidance Actually Say

You don't have to take anyone's word for the core advice, because it's written into the official documents.

- **The Abilify Medication Guide** (the leaflet that comes with the prescription in the US) tells patients to **avoid drinking alcohol** while taking Abilify.
- The same guide says not to drive, operate heavy machinery, or do other dangerous activities until you know how Abilify affects you.
- The prescribing information lists warnings that alcohol can make worse: sleepiness, orthostatic hypotension, falls, problems with body temperature regulation, seizures, and difficulty swallowing.
- Abilify carries the **boxed warning** shared by antidepressants about suicidal thoughts and behaviors in children, teens, and young adults, because of its use in depression. Alcohol is linked with low mood and impulsive acts, which is one more reason to be careful in younger people.

What the official documents **don't** do is give a safe number of drinks. There's no published threshold that says "two drinks on Abilify is fine." Anyone who gives you a precise allowance that applies to everyone is guessing. The realistic version is a conversation with your prescriber about your dose, your condition, and your drinking.

## Can You Drink on Abilify at All? The "Just One Drink" Question

This is what most people actually want to know. Here's an honest way to think about it.

**The official answer is no.** Avoiding alcohol is the label advice, and it's the safest choice.

**The real-world answer depends on you.** Many prescribers, in practice, are more concerned about regular or heavy drinking than about a single drink at a wedding for someone who has been stable on a low dose for months. Whether that applies to you depends on things like:

- **Your dose.** Someone on 2 to 5 mg as an add-on for depression is in a different spot from someone on 20 to 30 mg for schizophrenia or acute mania.
- **How long you've been on it.** In the first few weeks, and after any dose change, side effects like dizziness and sleepiness are more likely. That's the worst time to experiment.
- **What it's treating.** For bipolar disorder especially, alcohol is a well-known trigger for mood episodes and is linked with worse outcomes. Your prescriber may want you to avoid it completely for that reason alone.
- **Your other medicines.** Abilify is often taken with an antidepressant, a mood stabilizer, a sleep aid, or an anti-anxiety medicine. Each extra sedating drug raises the stakes.
- **Your history with alcohol.** If drinking has been a problem before, that changes the conversation entirely.

If you've talked to your prescriber and they're comfortable with an occasional drink, these habits keep the risk lower:

1. Have **one drink**, slowly, with a meal.
2. Drink water alongside it.
3. **Don't drive** or do anything that needs quick reactions afterward. Arrange a ride before you go out.
4. Stand up slowly, and be careful on stairs and in the bathroom at night.
5. Don't combine it with other sedating things that evening, like sleep aids, antihistamines, cannabis, or opioid painkillers.
6. Notice how you feel and be honest with yourself. If one drink hits much harder than it used to, that's useful information to pass on to your prescriber.

## Aripiprazole and Alcohol: Is the Generic Any Different?

No. Aripiprazole is the active ingredient in Abilify, and the generic tablets, the dissolving tablets, the oral solution, and the injections all contain the same drug. Everything in this article applies equally to "aripiprazole and alcohol." The only thing to check with the long-acting injections is timing: because the drug is released steadily for weeks, there's no "off" day when it's out of your system.

## Timing: How Long After Abilify Can You Drink?

This question usually comes from a reasonable idea: take your dose in the morning, drink in the evening, and the two won't overlap. Unfortunately, aripiprazole doesn't work that way.

- **Aripiprazole has a very long half-life,** around 75 hours according to the label, and its active breakdown product (dehydro-aripiprazole) lasts even longer, roughly 94 hours. A half-life is the time it takes for the amount in your body to fall by half.
- **It takes about two weeks to reach a steady level** in your blood. After that, the amount in your system is fairly constant across the whole day, every day.
- **Long-acting injections** keep a steady level for a month or more by design.

So once you're on regular dosing, there's no time of day when Abilify is "worn off." Spacing your dose and your drink by a few hours doesn't meaningfully separate them. The level of aripiprazole in your blood when you have a drink at 9 pm is close to the level at 9 am.

What timing *can* do is help with the alcohol side. Your body clears roughly one standard drink per hour, though that varies a lot. Waiting until the alcohol has fully cleared before driving, and before taking any other sedating medicine that night, is still sensible.

## Don't Skip or Stop Abilify So You Can Drink

Some people consider skipping a dose before a night out. It's a bad trade for two reasons.

First, it doesn't work. Because aripiprazole lasts so long in the body, one skipped dose barely changes the level in your blood. You'd still be drinking with Abilify on board.

Second, it can backfire. Missing doses, especially repeatedly, raises the chance that the symptoms you're being treated for come back: a manic or depressive episode, a return of psychosis, or a slide back into depression. Stopping antipsychotics suddenly can also cause withdrawal-type symptoms in some people. If you want more flexibility around alcohol, or you're not happy with the medicine, the right move is to talk with your prescriber about changing the plan, not to adjust it yourself.

## Alcohol, Mood, and the Conditions Abilify Treats

Even apart from the drug interaction, alcohol tends to work against what Abilify is trying to do.

**Bipolar disorder.** Alcohol use is common in people with bipolar disorder, and research has consistently linked it with more frequent mood episodes, worse sleep, and poorer response to treatment. Alcohol disrupts sleep, and sleep loss is a well-known trigger for mania. The "lift" of a few drinks can also blur the line between a good night and the start of a high.

**Depression.** Alcohol is a depressant. It can improve mood for an hour and then drag it down for a day or two after. Many people notice their worst low days follow drinking. If you're on Abilify because an antidepressant alone wasn't enough, drinking regularly can make it hard for you and your doctor to tell whether the treatment is working. Our guide to [antidepressants and alcohol](/never-hungover/antidepressants-and-alcohol) covers how alcohol interacts with the antidepressants Abilify is usually paired with.

**Anxiety and the morning after.** The jittery, dread-filled feeling after drinking (often called "hangxiety") is partly a rebound effect as alcohol wears off. If you're already prone to anxiety or restlessness, that rebound can be stronger. See our [hangxiety guide](/never-hungover/hangxiety-complete-guide-2026-supplements-research) for what's behind it.

**Schizophrenia and psychosis.** Alcohol can worsen symptoms, interfere with sticking to treatment, and raise the risk of relapse. The added sedation and impaired judgment matter more when someone's thinking is already under strain.

### What about using aripiprazole to cut down on drinking?

You may come across research testing aripiprazole as a treatment for alcohol use disorder, based on its effects on the brain's dopamine reward system. Results have been mixed, and it isn't approved for that use. That research doesn't mean it's safe to drink on Abilify, and it doesn't mean the medicine will reduce your cravings. If you'd like help cutting back, there are medicines approved for that, and your doctor can talk them through with you.

## Abilify, Alcohol, and Blackouts

People sometimes search for this after a night where they remember much less than they expected. There's limited formal research on blackouts with aripiprazole specifically. What we do know is that blackouts are mainly driven by how quickly your blood alcohol rises, and that anything sedating which acts on the brain can make the effects of a given amount of alcohol feel stronger. Combining alcohol with other sedating medicines, which people on Abilify often take too, raises that risk further.

If you've had a blackout while on Abilify, treat it as a sign that the combination is affecting you more than you realize, and mention it to your prescriber. Our article on [blacking out from drinking](/never-hungover/blackout-drunk) explains what's happening in the brain during a blackout.

## Abilify and Alcohol Side Effects to Watch For

These are the effects most likely to show up or get worse when you drink on Abilify:

| Effect | Why it happens | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| Unusual drowsiness or feeling "too drunk" | Both slow the brain | Stop drinking, stay with someone, don't drive |
| Dizziness or fainting when standing | Both lower blood pressure; alcohol dehydrates | Sit or lie down, rise slowly, drink water |
| Unsteadiness and falls | Sedation plus low blood pressure | Avoid stairs and baths; have someone nearby |
| Restlessness or poor sleep afterward | Akathisia plus alcohol's sleep disruption | Tell your prescriber if it keeps happening |
| Low mood or anxiety the next day | Alcohol rebound on top of a mood condition | Track it; mention it at your next visit |
| Strong urges to gamble, spend, or binge eat | Known label warning, inhibitions lowered | Tell your prescriber; dose changes often help |
| Overheating | Impaired temperature control plus dehydration | Get somewhere cool, hydrate, seek help if confused |

## Warning Signs: When to Get Help Right Away

Most people who have a drink on Abilify will just feel sleepier than usual. But some signs mean you should stop waiting and get help.

**Call 911 or go to the emergency room if someone on Abilify who has been drinking:**

- Can't be woken up, or keeps drifting off and can't stay awake
- Is breathing very slowly, irregularly, or making snoring or gurgling sounds while unresponsive
- Vomits while very drowsy (lay them on their side so they don't choke; difficulty swallowing is a listed side effect of aripiprazole)
- Faints, or falls and hits their head
- Has a seizure
- Develops a **high fever with stiff muscles, confusion, sweating, or a racing heart**. This can be neuroleptic malignant syndrome, a rare but serious reaction to antipsychotics, and it needs emergency care.
- Talks about hurting themselves or seems at risk (call or text **988** in the US, or 911)

For questions about a possible overdose or a mixture of medicines and alcohol, you can call **Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222** (US) at any time. If you're unsure whether someone has had a dangerous amount to drink, our guide to [alcohol poisoning signs](/never-hungover/alcohol-poisoning-signs) lists what to look for.

**Make a routine appointment with your prescriber if you notice:**

- Drinking has started to feel like the way you manage restlessness, sleep, or mood
- One or two drinks affect you much more than they used to
- New urges you find hard to control
- Your mood is less stable on weeks you drink

## Who Should Be Most Careful

You're at higher risk from combining Abilify and alcohol if you:

- **Recently started Abilify or changed your dose**, when dizziness and drowsiness are most likely
- **Take other sedating medicines**, such as benzodiazepines like Xanax, sleep aids, gabapentin, opioids, or sedating antihistamines
- **Have bipolar disorder**, where alcohol is a known trigger for mood episodes
- **Are over 65**, when falls and low blood pressure are more dangerous (and the label has a boxed warning about antipsychotic use in older people with dementia)
- **Have a seizure disorder**, since both aripiprazole and alcohol withdrawal can lower the seizure threshold
- **Drink heavily or binge**, or have struggled with alcohol before
- **Drive for work** or operate machinery

If any of these describe you, have a frank conversation with your prescriber or pharmacist. For a wider look at how common medicines and supplements interact with alcohol, see our [DHM medication interactions and safety guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025). If you also take a sleep-focused antipsychotic, our [Seroquel and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/seroquel-and-alcohol) covers that combination, and our [Xanax and alcohol](/never-hungover/xanax-and-alcohol) and [gabapentin and alcohol](/never-hungover/gabapentin-and-alcohol) guides cover two common add-ons.

## What About Hangover Supplements Like DHM?

If you're on Abilify, the safest hangover plan is the simplest one: drink little or nothing, eat beforehand, drink water, and sleep. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits with the best evidence.

Some readers ask about DHM (dihydromyricetin), a plant compound sold as a hangover supplement. Here's the honest picture for someone on Abilify:

- Most DHM research comes from animal and lab studies, with only limited human data. There is no good evidence that it prevents hangovers reliably in people.
- In animal studies, DHM acts on GABA-A receptors in the brain, the same system alcohol affects. That's part of why it's studied, but it also means you shouldn't assume it's neutral alongside other brain-active medicines.
- **There are no studies of DHM combined with aripiprazole.** No one can tell you the combination is safe, because it hasn't been tested.
- DHM does **not** cancel out the drowsiness, dizziness, or judgment effects of mixing Abilify and alcohol. It won't make it safe to drive.

If you're curious about DHM, ask your prescriber or pharmacist first and bring the product label with you. Don't start it on your own while you're on an antipsychotic.

## The Bottom Line

- The Abilify Medication Guide says to **avoid alcohol**. That's the safest choice.
- The interaction isn't a chemical reaction in the blood. It's added drowsiness, dizziness, impaired judgment, and a higher risk of falls, plus alcohol working against the mood or thinking problems Abilify treats.
- Aripiprazole lasts days in your body, so **timing your dose around a drink doesn't separate them**, and skipping doses to drink can bring symptoms back.
- If your prescriber is comfortable with an occasional drink, keep it to one, with food and water, and never drive afterward.
- Get emergency help for someone who can't be woken, is breathing poorly, faints, has a seizure, or develops a high fever with stiff muscles.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you drink alcohol while taking Abilify?**

The Abilify Medication Guide advises avoiding alcohol. Both alcohol and aripiprazole affect the brain, and together they can increase drowsiness, dizziness, and impaired judgment, and raise the risk of falls. Some prescribers are comfortable with an occasional single drink for someone who's been stable on a low dose, but that's an individual decision to make with your own prescriber, not a general rule.

**What happens if you drink on Abilify?**

Most commonly, you feel more drowsy, dizzy, or drunk than you'd expect from the amount you had, and you may feel light-headed when you stand up. Alcohol can also worsen restlessness and sleep and make mood less stable over the following days. Rarely, heavy drinking on Abilify can lead to dangerous sedation, fainting, or falls. If someone can't be woken or is breathing poorly, call 911.

**How long after taking Abilify can I drink alcohol?**

There's no safe gap within a day. Aripiprazole has a half-life of about 75 hours, and after roughly two weeks of regular dosing its level in your blood stays fairly steady around the clock. Taking your dose in the morning and drinking at night doesn't meaningfully separate them. If you stop Abilify, it takes many days to clear, and you should only stop under your prescriber's guidance.

**Should I skip my Abilify dose if I'm going to drink?**

No. Because aripiprazole stays in the body so long, skipping one dose barely changes the amount in your system, so it doesn't make drinking safer. Missing doses can raise the chance of your symptoms returning. If you want more flexibility around alcohol, talk with your prescriber about your treatment plan instead.

**Is aripiprazole and alcohol different from Abilify and alcohol?**

No. Aripiprazole is the active ingredient in Abilify, so generic tablets, dissolving tablets, liquid, and long-acting injections like Abilify Maintena and Aristada all carry the same alcohol advice. With the injections, the drug is released steadily for weeks, so there's no point at which it's out of your system.

**Can Abilify and alcohol cause blackouts?**

There's little research on blackouts with aripiprazole specifically. Blackouts are mainly driven by how fast blood alcohol rises, but sedating medicines that act on the brain can make a given amount of alcohol hit harder, and many people on Abilify take other sedating medicines too. If you've blacked out while on Abilify, tell your prescriber, since it suggests the combination affects you more than you realize.

**Does alcohol make Abilify less effective?**

Alcohol doesn't significantly change how your liver breaks down aripiprazole, so it isn't known to lower the drug's level in your blood. But it can work against the treatment itself: alcohol worsens sleep, can trigger mood episodes in bipolar disorder, deepens low mood in depression, and makes it harder for you and your doctor to tell whether the medicine is working.

**Is it safe to take DHM while on Abilify?**

There are no studies of DHM combined with aripiprazole, so no one can say the combination is safe. DHM acts on brain GABA receptors in animal studies, so it's not a neutral add-on to brain-active medicines. It also doesn't reduce the drowsiness or impairment from mixing Abilify and alcohol. Ask your prescriber or pharmacist before trying it.
